summary: Supply the cash back limit, the amount purchased and the cash back and the Cash back calculator solves for cash back with limit. Think of it as a shortcut for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Cash back calculator work?
sections.html:
The Cash back calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports cash back with limit in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case; then you type in the cash back limit, the amount purchased and the cash back.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Cash back calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Cash back with limit=the smaller of (cash back limit, amount purchased × percentage cash back)
Percentage cash back=cash back ÷ amount purchased

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Cash back limit = 10, Amount purchased = 10 and Percentage cash back = 10 %. Working through the relationship above gives Cash back = 1 and Cash back with limit = 1.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Cash back = 1 and Cash back with limit = 1 should be roughly the size you expected from Cash back limit = 10 and Amount purchased = 10.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in US Dollar, and convertible to any of the 113 units on that chip.
  • Shown in percent, and convertible to any of the 6 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • %, opening in percent
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Cash back calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Sizing up a purchase before you commit to it
  • Comparing two offers that quote their costs in different ways
  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the cash back limit, the amount purchased and the cash back — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the Cash back calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns cash back with limit, derived from the cash back limit, the amount purchased and the cash back. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Cash back calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the cash back limit, the amount purchased and the cash back, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter cash back limit in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Cash back limit opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Cash back = 1. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Cash back calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
